teach.say: A subprogram is a named piece of a program you can use again. def gives the piece a name, and the indented lines under it belong to that name. Writing the name with brackets after it runs those lines, and that is called calling it. A subprogram that only displays things, like this one, is called a procedure.

questions.q: Change the program so the procedure is handed 7 instead of 4.

questions.fb: A parameter is the name the subprogram gives to whatever it is handed. The value handed over at the call is the argument.

c = input()

Use the parameter's own name inside the procedure, and the procedure works for any value handed in.

questions.fb: A parameter is a name that only exists inside the subprogram. Nothing else in the program can see it, and it cannot see any other name instead.

questions.q: Ask the user for two words, one on each line. Write a procedure called pair that takes two words and displays [first word] and [second word]. Call pair with the words in the order typed, then call it again with them the other way round.

Two lines of output.

Write a procedure with two parameters.
Call it once with the first word first.
Call it again with the second word first.

questions.starter: # Two parameters, two calls, opposite orders
require: This one needs a procedure called pair, written with def.

tests.why: The same procedure gives both lines. Two identical lines means both calls handed the values over the same way round.
With the same word twice the two lines match, which is correct here.
The words are never written inside the procedure, so swapping them is done in the call.

questions.fb: Arguments are matched to parameters by their order, not by their names. Swapping them in the call is all it takes to swap the output.

questions.q: Press Run. This subprogram works something out and hands the answer back.

teach.say: Some subprograms work a value out and hand it back instead of displaying it. return is the word that hands it back. A subprogram that hands a value back is called a function, and the value it hands back is its return value.

brief: Nothing is marked on this one.
Notice that triple displays nothing of its own.
questions.starter:
def triple(n):
    return n * 3
answer = triple(4)
print(answer)
print(triple(10))
lines: Name a function triple, with one parameter called n.
Work out three times n and hand that value back.
Call triple with 4, and keep what comes back in answer.
Show what answer is holding.
Call triple with 10 and show what comes back straight away.
questions.fb: return gives the value to the line that called the function. That line then decides whether to store it or display it.

questions.q: What will this program display?
brief: Read every line before you choose.

teach.say: What a function hands back is an ordinary value, so it can be stored in a variable and that variable can be handed back in again.

questions.fb: a is 7, so add_on(a) is add_on(7), which hands back 9. A return value can be used anywhere an ordinary value can.

questions.q: Change the last line so the value double hands back is displayed.

Change only the last line.
Display exactly: 14
One line of output.

hint.think: Running the function is not the same as doing something with its answer.

require: Keep the function and display what it hands back.

tests.why: Nothing came out at all. The function worked the answer out and handed it back, and then the program threw it away.

questions.fb: A function's return value is lost unless the caller uses it. print() round the call is the shortest way of using it.

questions.q: Finish the function so it hands its answer back to the line that called it.

teach.say: return goes in front of the value being handed back, and the line is indented like every other line of the subprogram.

brief: The user types one whole number.
Replace ____ with the one word that hands a value back.
Display the number doubled, and nothing else.
One line of output.

n = int(input())
def double(x):

print(double(n))

tests.why: Python stopped at the ____. The word that hands a value back goes in its place.

The function does the multiplying for any value it is handed.

questions.fb: Without return a function hands nothing back, however much work it does inside.

tests.why: Nothing displayed means the function returns the answer but the main program never used it.
Zero doubled is zero, and it still has to be displayed.
Negative numbers double in the same way.

questions.q: This program should display the number typed, doubled. Find the mistake and put it right.
brief: Press Run first and read what comes out.

One line of output.

walk: The word None means the function handed nothing back.
Working a value out and handing it back are two different jobs.
One word is missing from the indented line.

questions.starter:
n = int(input())
def double(x):
    x * 2
print(double(n))
require: A function hands its answer back, so this one needs return.

tests.why: The word None came out. The function worked out x * 2 and then threw it away, because no return hands it back.

Add the missing word in front of the sum and the function works for any number.

questions.fb: None is Python's word for no value at all. A function with no return hands back None every time, however much it worked out.

questions.q: Ask the user for a whole number. Write a function called double that returns twice the number it is handed. Keep what double hands back in a variable and display it. Then hand that variable to double and display what comes back on the next line.

questions.starter: # One function, called twice, the second time on its own answer
require: This one needs a function called double, written with def.
A function hands its answer back, so this one needs return.

Zero stays zero both times, and both lines must still appear.
Negative numbers double twice in the same way.
If line 2 was 100 as well, the second call was handed the original number again.

questions.q: Press Run. Two subprograms work out the same answer in two different ways.

teach.say: A procedure displays something and hands nothing back. A function hands a value back and displays nothing. print shows a value on the screen; return gives it to the line that called the subprogram.

brief: Nothing is marked on this one.
Both lines of output say 10, but only one of the subprograms displayed it.
questions.starter:
def show_it(n):
    print(n * 2)
def give_it(n):
    return n * 2
show_it(5)
answer = give_it(5)
print(answer)
lines: Name the first subprogram show_it, with one parameter.
It displays twice that value itself, so it is a procedure.
Name the second subprogram give_it, also with one parameter.
It hands twice that value back instead, so it is a function.
Calling show_it displays 10 straight away.
Calling give_it hands 10 back, so it is kept in answer.
Show what answer is holding.
questions.fb: OCR asks for this difference by name: a function returns a value and a procedure does not. The work inside them can be exactly the same.

questions.q: What will this program display?
brief: Read every line before you choose.

a = area(5, 4)
print("area " + str(a))
require: A function hands its answer back, so this one needs return.

tests.why: Two lines came out: a bare 20 from the print inside area, and then area None, because nothing was handed back.

questions.fb: One word turns a procedure into a function. print displays the value and hands back nothing; return hands it back and displays nothing.

questions.q: Finish the program so the value the function hands back is kept in cost.

teach.say: A call can go anywhere a value can go, including on the right of an = sign.

teach.say: A function can hand back a word just as easily as a number, and an if inside it can decide which word to hand back.

Ask whether the value is 50 or more.
If it is, hand back the word pass.
Otherwise take the other path.
On that path, hand back the word fail.
Call grade with 80 and display what comes back.

band displays nothing of its own.
One line of output, with one space after the word band.

39 is under 40. A line reading band None means one path of the if hands nothing back.

walk: One path hands a word back.

Exactly 40 takes the same path, so this one worked too.

questions.q: Ask the user for a word. Then ask for a whole number. Write a function called tag that returns the word high for a number of 40 or more and the word low for anything less. Write a procedure called show that takes a word and a tag and displays [word]: [tag].

hint.think: The function works out one of two words. The procedure makes the line. The main program joins them up with one call.
walk: Read the word, then read the number and cast it.
Write the function that chooses high or low.

Call the procedure, handing it the word and what the function gives back.

Make a local variable n and put 1 in it.
Show what the local n is holding.
In the main program, make a variable n holding 50.
Call count_up, which uses its own local n.
Show what the main program's n is holding.
questions.fb: The local n lives and dies inside count_up. The main program's n never knew it existed.

questions.q: What will this program display?
brief: Read every line before you choose.

teach.say: A subprogram is allowed to read a variable made outside it without doing anything special, as long as it does not try to change it.

questions.fb: Reading is free. The subprogram looked for limit, could not find a local one, and used the one outside instead.

questions.q: What will this program display?
brief: Read every line before you choose.

teach.say: To change a variable made outside it, a subprogram has to say global and the variable's name first. Without that line, the = makes a local variable instead.

score starts at 100, which is written into the program.

score = 100
def add_on():

add_on()

tests.why: Python stopped at the ____. The word that lets a subprogram change an outside variable goes in its place.

The procedure reads n without any fuss, because reading needs no global.

questions.q: Ask the user for a whole number and keep it in a variable called total. Write a procedure called boost that puts 99 in its own variable called total and displays it. Call boost, then display the main program's total on the next line.

Two lines of output, with the 99 first.
boost takes nothing in its brackets.
The main program's total must still hold what was typed.

hint.think: A variable given a value inside a subprogram is local, so it does not need to avoid the name total.

questions.starter: # Two variables, one name, two different lives
require: This one needs a procedure called boost, written with def.

tests.why: The 5 survives. A second line of 99 means global total was used, so the main program's variable was changed instead.
Zero is still the main program's value afterwards.
A crash here usually means int() was left out on the way in.
If the lines came out the other way round, boost was called after the second line was displayed.

questions.fb: Two variables can share a name without sharing anything else. The local one inside boost is thrown away the moment boost finishes.

questions.q: This program should add 2 to the total once for every turn, then display the total. Find the mistake and put it right.
brief: Press Run first and type 3, then read the last line of the error message.
Do not change the loop or the number 2.
The total starts at 0, which is written into the program.
A number of 0 turns means the total stays at 0.

hint.think: The subprogram is trying to change a variable that belongs to the main program.
walk: Python sees total = on a line inside the subprogram.
So it treats total as local and finds it empty.
One line at the top of the subprogram puts that right.

questions.starter:
total = 0
turns = int(input())
def add_on():
    total = total + 2
for i in range(turns):
    add_on()
print(total)
require: Changing a variable that belongs to the main program needs global.

tests.why: The error says total was used before it was given a value. Inside the subprogram it is a local name until global says otherwise.
Three turns at 2 each. If you got 2, the total is being set back to 0 somewhere each turn.
No turns, so the subprogram never runs and the starting 0 is displayed. This one already worked.

questions.fb: An UnboundLocalError means Python made a local variable of that name and then found nothing in it. global tells it to use the outside one instead.

questions.q: Ask the user for a whole number of turns. Write a procedure called up that adds 3 to a total the whole program shares. Write a procedure called down that takes 1 away from that same total. Call up and then down once for every turn, then display the total.
brief: The user types one whole number, which is never below 0.
The total starts at 0, which is written into the program.
Neither procedure displays anything.
One line of output, holding the final total.

hint.think: Both procedures change one variable that lives in the main program, so both need the same declaration.
walk: Make the total in the main program and set it to 0.

questions.fb: A variable the whole program can see is called global. Two subprograms can share one, which is powerful and is also why a shared variable is easy to lose track of.

questions.q: What will this program display?
brief: Read every line before you choose.

teach.say: A call inside a loop happens once every time round the loop, and what the function hands back can be added to a running total.

questions.fb: The loop gives i the values 0, 1 and 2, so step hands back 10, 11 and 12. Those three add up to 33.

questions.q: Finish the program so each number typed is worth twice its value in the total.

teach.say: A call can sit on the right of a + just as a variable can, because what it hands back is an ordinary value.

brief: The user types how many numbers there are, then that many whole numbers.
Replace ____ with a call to points, handing it the number just read.

A count of 0 means no numbers are read at all.

questions.starter:
def points(n):
    return n * 2
count = int(input())
total = 0
for i in range(count):
    n = int(input())
    total = total + ____
print(total)
require: Keep the function and call it inside the loop.

tests.why: Six and eight make 14. Python stopped at the ____, so put the call there.
One number, worth nothing, so the total is 0.
No numbers at all, so the loop never runs and the starting total is displayed.
Three numbers worth 2 each. A total of 2 means the call is outside the loop.

questions.fb: The loop decides how many times. The function deals with one number at a time. Neither one needs to know about the other.

questions.fb: A function does whatever the data type allows. Casting on the way in, with int(), is still your job in a program full of subprograms.

points is called once for each number, inside the loop.

require: This one needs a function called points, written with def.
A function hands its answer back, so this one needs return.

questions.fb: One subprogram, used once per item. The loop handles how many there are and the function handles one at a time.

require: This one needs a function called base, written with def.
This one needs a function called whole, written with def.

questions.fb: Subprograms call subprograms. Each one only has to do its own small job, which is how a long program is broken into short ones.
